title: Ubiquitin and Regulated Proteolysis as Signals

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A {{c1::degron}} is the feature the tagging machinery recognizes on a target: a short sequence, a chemical change or both.
cards.quote: A degron is the feature the tagging machinery recognizes on a target: a short sequence, a chemical change or both.
cards.section: One recognition step can change a protein's fate

cards.front: What is ubiquitin, and what does the proteasome do with a protein that carries an appropriate ubiquitin signal?
cards.back: Ubiquitin is a small protein, 76 amino acids long, attached to other proteins as a tag. The proteasome, a barrel-shaped protease, destroys proteins carrying an appropriate ubiquitin signal.
cards.quote: Ubiquitin is a small protein, 76 amino acids long, attached to other proteins as a tag.
cards.section: One recognition step can change a protein's fate

cards.front: In regulated ubiquitin pathways, how does a signal change a protein's fate?
cards.back: By changing what an E3 can recognize. A signal may complete a degron or strengthen an E3-target contact.
cards.quote: Signals change protein fate by changing what an E3 can recognize.
cards.section: One recognition step can change a protein's fate

cards.front: Why is regulated proteolysis a more costly-to-reverse signal than phosphorylation?
cards.back: A phosphate can be removed, and a ubiquitin mark can be cut off before degradation. Once the protein is cut into peptides, only a newly made copy replaces it.
cards.quote: Once a protein is cut into peptides, only a newly made copy replaces it.
cards.section: One recognition step can change a protein's fate

cards.front: What does E1 do at the start of the ubiquitin relay, and what bond does it form?
cards.back: E1 spends ATP to join ubiquitin's carboxyl end, glycine 76, to one of its own cysteines, forming a thioester (an energy-rich sulfur-carbonyl bond).
cards.quote: E1, the activating enzyme, spends ATP to join ubiquitin's carboxyl end, glycine 76, to one of its own cysteines.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: In the lesson's examples, which step of the E1, E2, E3 relay carries most of the target specificity, and why?
cards.back: The E3 (or its substrate receptor), the main selector though not the only one. One E1 supplies nearly the whole system, while each of roughly six hundred predicted E3s recognizes a set of degrons.
cards.quote: One E1 supplies nearly the whole system, while each E3 recognizes a set of degrons.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: E3 usually completes ubiquitin transfer by an {{c1::isopeptide}} bond: an amide between ubiquitin's C-terminus and a target lysine side chain rather than the backbone.
cards.quote: E3, the ligase, completes the transfer, usually by an isopeptide bond: an amide between ubiquitin's C-terminus and a target lysine side chain rather than the backbone.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: How do RING-type and HECT-type E3 ligases differ in handling ubiquitin?
cards.back: A RING-type ligase holds loaded E2 beside the target so ubiquitin passes directly across. A HECT-type ligase first takes ubiquitin onto its own cysteine, then passes it to the target.
cards.quote: A RING-type ligase holds loaded E2 beside the target, so ubiquitin passes directly across.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: An E3 is mixed with ubiquitin-loaded E2. Before the target receives ubiquitin, the E3 itself carries ubiquitin as a short-lived thioester on one of its own cysteines. Is it RING-type or HECT-type?
cards.back: HECT-type. It accepts ubiquitin from E2 onto its catalytic cysteine, then transfers it to the target.
cards.why: A RING ligase never holds ubiquitin itself; it promotes direct transfer from E2 to the target.
cards.quote: A HECT-type ligase first takes ubiquitin onto its own cysteine.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: In an SCF ligase, a cullin scaffold holds a small RING protein that docks E2, the adaptor {{c1::Skp1}} and an interchangeable F-box protein that binds the degron.
cards.quote: SCF ligases are RING-type: a cullin scaffold holds a small RING protein that docks E2, the adaptor Skp1 and an interchangeable F-box protein that binds the degron.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: What kind of ubiquitin chain is a usual signal for proteasomal destruction?
cards.back: A chain joined through lysine 48 and at least four ubiquitins long.
cards.quote: A chain joined through lysine 48 and at least four ubiquitins long is a usual proteasome signal.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: A protein carries a chain of ubiquitins joined through lysine 63 instead of lysine 48. Is proteasomal destruction the likely outcome?
cards.back: No. The lysine-48 chain is the usual proteasome signal. A lysine-63 chain is more likely read by proteins with ubiquitin-binding domains, as a scaffold or trafficking signal.
cards.why: Linkage, length and branching shape how a mark is read.
cards.quote: Linkage, length and branching shape how a mark is read.
cards.section: The bonds and branches behind the relay

cards.front: How does phosphorylation of an inhibitor lead to its destruction through β-TrCP?
cards.back: A signal-activated kinase phosphorylates both serines of a short degron. β-TrCP binds only the doubly phosphorylated sequence and brings the inhibitor to an SCF for a lysine-48 chain and proteasomal destruction.
cards.quote: The F-box protein β-TrCP binds only when both serines are phosphorylated.

cards.front: Both degron serines of a β-TrCP target are replaced by alanines, but the kinase and proteasome still work. Which step fails first, and why?
cards.back: Phosphorylation fails first: alanine has no hydroxyl, so the kinase cannot add phosphates. Without them β-TrCP cannot recognize the degron, so the inhibitor never reaches the SCF.
cards.quote: Both degron serines are replaced by alanines, but the kinase and proteasome still work. What step fails first?

cards.front: A GFP-tagged 9-residue segment with two serines has a half-life of 10 minutes after cycloheximide blocks new synthesis; with a kinase inhibitor it is 60 minutes. Serine-to-alanine mutants have a 60-minute half-life with or without the inhibitor. Serine-to-aspartate mutants have a 15-minute half-life even with the inhibitor. What fraction of the unmutated fusion remains after 30 minutes without the inhibitor, and what do the results show?
cards.back: One-eighth remains (three half-lives of 10 minutes). The segment is a degron that works when the serines carry negative charge, so phosphorylation by the kinase creates it.
cards.why: Aspartate mimics phosphate and destabilizes even without the kinase; alanine cannot be phosphorylated and is stable.
cards.quote: The reversible phosphate reads the signal; destruction commits that target molecule.

cards.front: For IκB and for β-catenin, how does the signal act on the phosphorylation that creates the degron, and what is the result for each protein under signal?
cards.back: For an IκB-type inhibitor, the signal activates a kinase that adds the phosphates, so the inhibitor is destroyed. For β-catenin the signal stops phosphorylation, so it is no longer recognized and is not destroyed. Both rest on the same logic: the phosphate-dependent degron decides E3 recognition.
cards.quote: The Wnt lesson uses the same logic for β-catenin, except its signal stops phosphorylation.

cards.front: What do prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) add to HIF-1α, and what does the reaction need?
cards.back: A hydroxyl on a proline, which completes a docking site for VHL. The reaction needs iron, 2-oxoglutarate and one molecule of oxygen.
cards.quote: The reaction needs iron, 2-oxoglutarate and one molecule of oxygen.

cards.front: Why does oxygen sensing through PHDs need no separate oxygen receptor?
cards.back: Oxygen is a substrate of the PHD reaction, used up like flour in bread, so the enzyme's own output reports how much oxygen there is.
cards.quote: Oxygen is a substrate, used up like flour in bread; no separate oxygen receptor is required.

cards.front: Why does HIF-1α build up when oxygen falls?
cards.back: Falling oxygen lowers how often PHDs finish the hydroxylation, so VHL has less to grip. Destruction slows while HIF-1α synthesis continues.
cards.quote: Falling oxygen lowers how often PHDs finish the reaction, so VHL has less to grip and HIF-1α builds up while synthesis continues.

cards.front: A cultured cell lacks working VHL, has a normal HIF1A gene and normal PHDs, and is grown in 21 percent oxygen. What happens to HIF-1α?
cards.back: It is hydroxylated but not ubiquitinated, so it accumulates and its target genes are on.
cards.why: VHL is the substrate receptor that reads the hydroxyproline, so without it no chain is built.
cards.quote: VHL, the substrate receptor of a cullin-RING ligase, plays the role an F-box protein plays in an SCF, so it had to be reading some degron on HIF-1α.

cards.front: A drug removes the iron PHDs need, and cells with working VHL are grown in air. What happens to HIF-1α and why?
cards.back: HIF-1α accumulates and its genes switch on even in air. Without iron the PHD reaction cannot finish, so there is no hydroxyproline for VHL to recognize.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the PHD reaction needs iron, 2-oxoglutarate and oxygen.
cards.quote: The reaction needs iron, 2-oxoglutarate and one molecule of oxygen.

cards.front: A HIF-1α peptide with an ordinary proline at 564 does not bind purified VHL. The same peptide made with hydroxyproline binds tightly with no cell extract. The ordinary peptide gains binding after incubation with extract plus oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate. What do these results show?
cards.back: VHL recognizes the hydroxylated proline, and the extract holds an oxygen-using enzyme that makes it.
cards.why: The synthetic hydroxyproline peptide binds with no extract; the ordinary peptide needs the PHD ingredients.
cards.quote: The film's peptide test named it: a hydroxylated proline, recognized with no cell extract present.

cards.front: Once HIF-1α accumulates, what does it do in the nucleus?
cards.back: It pairs with ARNT and switches on genes including VEGF, a growth factor that drives new blood vessels.
cards.quote: It pairs with ARNT in the nucleus and switches on genes including VEGF, a growth factor that drives new blood vessels.

cards.front: In the PHD reaction, where do the two atoms of one O2 molecule end up?
cards.back: One oxygen atom enters the new hydroxyl on proline. The other enters succinate when 2-oxoglutarate loses carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: One oxygen atom enters the new hydroxyl. The other enters succinate when 2-oxoglutarate loses carbon dioxide.

cards.front: For a protein made at constant rate s and destroyed with first-order rate constant k, at steady state P = {{c1::s/k}}.
cards.back: dP/dt = s − k × P; half-life = 0.69/k.
cards.quote: dP/dt = s − k × P; at steady state P = s/k; half-life = 0.69/k.

cards.front: A protein is made at 40 molecules per minute and destroyed by first-order kinetics with a half-life of 14 minutes (take ln 2 as 0.7). What is the steady-state amount per cell?
cards.back: About 800 molecules. k = 0.7/14 = 0.05 per minute, so P = s/k = 40/0.05 = 800.
cards.quote: Let a protein amount, P, be made at constant rate s and destroyed with first-order rate constant k: dP/dt = s − k × P; at steady state P = s/k; half-life = 0.69/k.

cards.front: Synthesis stays fixed while the destruction rate constant k falls to half its original value. What happens to steady-state P and the half-life?
cards.back: Both double. The steady state becomes s/(k/2) = 2s/k, and the half-life becomes 0.69/(k/2), twice 0.69/k.
cards.quote: Synthesis stays fixed while k falls to half its original value. What happens to steady-state P and the half-life?

cards.front: In a simple model, a transcription factor has a five-minute half-life in air, so its steady pool is s/k, about seven minutes of synthesis. Oxygen falls, destruction stops completely and synthesis continues. Roughly how large is the pool relative to baseline after 30 minutes?
cards.back: About five times baseline. k is about 0.14 per minute, so each minute adds s, about 14 percent of the s/k baseline; 30 minutes adds about 4.2 times baseline to the original 1.
cards.why: Rests on P = s/k and on destruction stopping while synthesis continues.
cards.quote: After 30 minutes the pool is about five times baseline, without waiting for new transcription.

cards.front: Why design an oxygen-responsive transcription factor to be made continuously and destroyed continuously, rather than made on demand? What does it cost?
cards.back: Stopping destruction raises the pool within minutes, while on-demand making would wait tens of minutes to hours for transcription, RNA processing and translation. In the lesson's simple model, destruction also makes the off-switch as fast as the on-switch: with a five-minute half-life, about 3 percent of the excess remains after 25 minutes. The cost is ATP and amino acids spent on discarded protein.
cards.quote: Continuous destruction also makes the off-switch as fast as the on-switch: when oxygen returns, the excess above baseline halves every five minutes

cards.front: A deubiquitinating enzyme removes a target's lysine-48 chain before the proteasome engages it. Can that protein molecule still be rescued? What if proteolysis has already begun?
cards.back: Before engagement, yes: removing the chain rescues that molecule from this destruction signal. Once proteolysis has cut the protein, removing ubiquitin cannot rebuild it; a replacement must be made.
cards.quote: A deubiquitinating enzyme removes a target's lysine-48 chain before the proteasome engages it. Can the same protein molecule still be rescued?

cards.front: {{c1::SUMO}}, a small ubiquitin-like modifier of about 100 amino acids, is attached to lysines by its own E1, E2 and E3 and usually changes binding or location.
cards.quote: SUMO, a small ubiquitin-like modifier of about 100 amino acids, is folded like ubiquitin and attached to lysines by its own E1, E2 and E3.

cards.front: In plants, how does auxin act as a molecular glue on TIR1 and Aux/IAA repressors?
cards.back: Auxin sits where TIR1, an F-box protein of an SCF, and an Aux/IAA repressor meet, strengthening their contact so the repressor is ubiquitinated and destroyed and auxin-responsive genes turn on.
cards.quote: A 2007 crystal structure from Mark Estelle's group with Ning Zheng confirmed the film's picture: auxin sits where TIR1 and an Aux/IAA repressor meet.
cards.section: Evidence that TIR1 is receptor and selector

cards.front: Auxin and TIR1 bind normally in a plant cell, but the proteasome is blocked. Will the Aux/IAA repressor disappear and the genes switch on by this route?
cards.back: No. Recognition and ubiquitination can occur, but the repressor remains if the proteasome cannot destroy it, so the genes stay off.
cards.quote: Auxin and TIR1 bind normally, but the proteasome is blocked. Will the repressor disappear and the genes switch on by this route?
cards.section: Evidence that TIR1 is receptor and selector

cards.front: A TIR1 variant grips an Aux/IAA repressor tightly with no auxin present, and still joins the SCF. Predict the state of auxin-responsive genes without auxin, and name the rule you used.
cards.back: The repressor would likely be ubiquitinated and destroyed without auxin, so the genes would likely be on without the hormone (extending the rule, not stated in the lesson). Rule: auxin works as glue that tightens TIR1's grip on the repressor; a signal changes protein fate by changing what the E3 can recognize.
cards.quote: The film called auxin a molecular glue, a small molecule that strengthens or creates a protein-protein contact.
cards.section: Evidence that TIR1 is receptor and selector

cards.front: How does lenalidomide cause destruction of Ikaros and Aiolos?
cards.back: It binds cereblon, a cullin-RING substrate receptor, and reshapes its surface so it grips Ikaros and Aiolos, which it would otherwise ignore. They are then ubiquitinated and destroyed.
cards.quote: The drug reshapes cereblon's surface so it grips the transcription factors Ikaros and Aiolos, which it would otherwise ignore, and they are then ubiquitinated and destroyed.
cards.section: Evidence that TIR1 is receptor and selector

cards.front: What is a PROTAC, and how does one borrow VHL?
cards.back: A two-headed molecule: one end binds a target, the other binds a ligase such as VHL, using a small molecule built around the hydroxyproline VHL recognizes in HIF-1α.
cards.quote: PROTACs are two-headed molecules: one end binds a target, while the other binds a ligase such as VHL, using a small molecule built around the hydroxyproline VHL recognizes in HIF-1α.
cards.section: Evidence that TIR1 is receptor and selector
